extracted.intended_audience: immigration applicants, attorneys, advocates, and public commenters on DHS/USCIS rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evidentiary guidance the Department of Homeland Security (DHS/USCIS) proposes to use when determining whether an alien is likely to become a public charge, including required evidence, how factors are weighed, and examples of positive and negative indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Public charge determinations are made based on the totality of the circumstances, weighing multiple positive and negative factors together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will consider all relevant information (assets/resources, financial status, health insurance, education/skills, age, etc.) in combination rather than any single dispositive factor. The weight of each factor depends on the context, recency, and duration (e.g., how recently benefits were received, whether benefits were received for extended periods or multiple time periods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of Assets and Resources
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS would consider certain types of evidence about an alien’s household assets and resources when reviewing this factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically includes, but is not limited to: the alien’s annual gross household income (all sources before deductions), excluding income from public benefits; additional income from individuals not included in the alien’s household who physically reside with the alien and whose income will be relied on; additional continuing monthly or yearly income from other persons or sources (excluding public benefits); household cash assets and resources as reflected in checking and savings account statements in the last 12 months; and household non-cash assets convertible to cash within 12 months (e.g., net cash value of real estate holdings minus mortgage/loans, annuities, securities, retirement and educational accounts, and other readily convertible assets). DHS solicits comment on whether 125 percent of the FPG is an appropriate threshold and on other possible measures/thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of household income and a 125% FPG threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes using household income at or above 125 percent of the Federal Poverty Guidelines (FPG) as a standard and welcomes comments on this threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS would consider annual gross household income (excluding public benefits) and may include additional income from non-household individuals who reside with and support the alien. DHS requests studies or data supporting alternative measures or thresholds. Example calculation context: to avoid a negative determination for household income as a factor, an alien would need household assets/resources sufficient to offset shortfalls (example given elsewhere in the document: $36,875 in household assets/resources in a particular scenario).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of Financial Status (liabilities and public benefits reliance)
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS would review evidence of liabilities and any past or current reliance on public benefits to assess financial status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items DHS proposes to review include: evidence that the alien has applied for or received any public benefit (as defined in proposed 8 CFR 212.21(b)) on or after the effective date; certification/approval to receive public benefits on or after the effective date; evidence of application for or receipt of a fee waiver for immigration benefits after the effective date; credit histories and credit scores; and whether the alien has private health insurance or the financial resources to pay for medical costs associated with identified medical conditions. The presence of liabilities or past reliance on benefits is a negative indicator of ability to be self-sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of current or past receipt of public benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Current or past applications for or receipt of public benefits (cash and non-cash as defined) are generally negative factors in the totality of the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS views receipt of public benefits as indicative of weak financial status and increased likelihood of future reliance. The weight given depends on recency, duration (e.g., receipt for multiple years), and frequency (e.g., multiple discrete periods of receipt). Certification or preapproval for future benefits is also generally negative because it suggests continuation; however, an alien may rebut by providing documentation showing termination or changed circumstances (e.g., pending employment after graduation). DHS will review both cash and non-cash benefits. DHS notes longstanding policy to afford less weight to benefits received longer ago.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee waivers (vs. fee exemptions) as evidence of financial inability
rubrics_metrics.description: Requesting or receiving a USCIS fee waiver is proposed to be considered a negative factor because it suggests inability to pay; fee exemptions are not considered relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under INA section 286(m), USCIS may waive fees for applicants demonstrating 'inability to pay.' DHS would consider past receipt of a fee waiver as part of the financial status factor. Fee exemptions—statutorily or policy-based waivers for specific categories or forms (not affirmatively requested due to inability to pay)—would not be considered, as they do not reflect the applicant's inability to pay. DHS cited congressional concerns about fee waiver increases as supporting that fee waivers indicate dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit reports and scores
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS proposes to consider U.S. credit reports and credit scores (when available) as part of the financial status factor, interpreting higher scores as positive and lower scores as negative indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credit reports provide payment history, loans, current debt, collections, and other financial information; credit scores rate credit risk at a point in time. DHS would generally consider a credit score characterized as 'good' or better to be a positive factor (indicating likely self-sufficiency) and a poor credit report to be a negative factor. DHS recognizes many individuals lack a U.S. credit history; absence of a U.S. credit report would not necessarily be negative — USCIS may give positive weight to evidence of little/no debt and a history of timely payments. USCIS would not consider errors on a credit score that have been verified by the credit agency. DHS requests comments on whether to consider credit scores categorized less than 'good,' which types of credit reports to consider, and what credit-history information should be reviewed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of financial means to pay for medical costs (health insurance)
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS would consider whether an alien has the financial means to pay reasonably foreseeable medical costs, including possession of private health insurance, as part of the financial status factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having private health insurance is a positive factor. Health insurance provided through government employment is not treated as a public benefit and is a positive factor. Lack of health insurance or of financial resources to pay medical costs is a negative factor. Receipt of health insurance that qualifies as a public benefit within the past 36 months (recent or current) would generally be weighed heavily as a negative factor. DHS will nonetheless consider other assets/resources, earned benefits, education, skills, or support that may mitigate likelihood of becoming a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and skills (statutory mandatory factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Education and skills are mandatory statutory factors and DHS proposes to consider whether the alien’s education and skills are adequate to obtain or maintain employment sufficient to avoid becoming a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher educational credentials and skills are generally positive because they increase employability and reduce likelihood of benefit receipt. DHS cites data showing relationships between educational attainment and unemployment and between education and rates/duration of public benefit participation. Evidence such as degrees, professional certificates, or licenses that increase employment prospects are positive factors; DHS notes certificate/license holders had lower rates of non-cash means-tested benefit participation in cited analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recency, duration, and frequency as weighting heuristics
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing negative indicators (particularly benefit receipt), DHS proposes to weigh recency, duration, and frequency to determine the weight assigned to that factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: benefits received longer ago are given less weight; receipt over extended periods (e.g., stays of 37–48 months) or repeated receipt (e.g., 3 times in two years) would carry greater weight. Certification/preapproval for future benefits suggests likely continuation and is weighed accordingly, unless applicant documents termination or changed circumstances.
